A genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; in normal hearing the brief ~≤0.5-1 ms polarity-sensitive CM / stimulus artefact window gives a mirror image between polarities only early, after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural response dominates and condensation and rarefaction averages become superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural component is absent/desynchronised. The only stimulus-locked activity recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM / artefact. The classic alternating-polarity teaching therefore describes loss of normal convergence after ~1 ms.

Round 1 public responses split on how that loss is phrased:

C camp – colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: without a neural ABR to make the two polarities converge, the polarity-sensitive CM dominates the whole analysis window so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. persistence of mirror-image relation for >~1 ms, often >1-1.5-2-3 ms into the neural latency range where waves III-V would be expected. That persistence is the practical bedside sign that the recorded activity is non-neural. They note A is not the classic pattern and B is non-specific, and that a ≤1 ms mirror image is normal CM behaviour.

D camp – colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: the cochlear microphonic itself is a very short stimulus-locked receptor potential, physiologically confined to ≤~0.8-1.0 ms post-stimulus. With neural loss there is no polarity-invariant component to sustain a response beyond ~1 ms; beyond the CM window the trace is effectively absent/flat. Hence the demonstrable polarity inversion/mirror image is limited to the CM window ≤1 ms, with loss of reproducible waves III-V thereafter. A >1 ms mirror image would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator in the neural window which is not provided by the brief CM. They interpret the same physiology as loss of later polarity invariance and confinement of mirroring to ≤1 ms.

A and B are consistently dismissed as non-defining. E is unlikely.

Unresolved wording nuance remains: “mirror image persists >1 ms” is the clinical convention for describing the absence of normal polarity-invariant convergence after ~1 ms, whereas the biophysical CM duration is ≤1 ms. The question stem’s phrasing favors the classic teaching formulation C, while the D formulation emphasizes strict CM duration. The majority in round 1 public responses now support C, but the D argument about physiological CM duration remains a substantive counter-position to track.

Because there is no neural ABR to break the polarity sensitivity, the condensation vs rarefaction waveforms remain mirror images well into the time window where waves I-V would normally appear, i.e. polarity inversion persists for > ~1 ms. This is classically described as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-sensitive response beyond the normal ≤1 ms CM window with absent/reduced reproducible waves III-V despite present OAEs/CM.

Current round shows a majority C position. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 now explicitly state the classic alternating-polarity sign is a prolonged mirror-image >1 ms, loss of normal polarity invariance, with absent neural ABR despite preserved OAEs/CM. They note the ≤1 ms mirroring is the normal CM-limited behaviour, not the pathological sign.

The D camp, colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9, argues the CM is short-lived so mirroring is confined to ≤1 ms and after that the response is flat/absent. This conflates the physiological duration of the CM generator with the clinical observation of persistent polarity sensitivity in the neural window: the mirror-image relationship is observed to persist because the neural component that would normally make the traces superimposable is absent, not because CM itself lasts >1 ms.

Options A – peaks I and III present, V absent – and B – prolonged latencies of peaks I and III – are not the defining ABR polarity manifestation and are not specific for ANSD.

Remaining nuance is terminological about “mirror image persists >1 ms” meaning persistence of polarity sensitivity into the neural window vs literal CM amplitude >1 ms. Literature conventionally reports the former as the ANSD polarity sign i.e. C.

Current best belief remains C as the intended ABR manifestation of auditory neuropathy, with the ~12 vs 6 split in round 1 reflecting the normal-vs-pathological polarity description confusion, but the weight of argument and majority now favors C.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains dominated by the alternating-polarity / cochlear microphonic signature of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Core physiology that is now stable across both camps:

The split is on how to operationalise the polarity sign.

C camp - Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 - argues the pathophysiologically informative sign is loss of the normal polarity-insensitive superimposition after ~1 ms. With no neural ABR to make the two polarities converge, the recorded activity at high level is dominated by the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact. This is described classically as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-dependent relationship for > ~1 ms, often quoted as >1 ms up to 2-3 ms, with absent/reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM. The only stimulus-locked activity that remains in ANSD is that brief microphonic. Hence condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only within that very early microphonic window, roughly ≤1 ms, and beyond ~1 ms the response is effectively absent/flat because there is no neural synchrony to sustain a reproducible waveform. The hallmark is therefore a brief early polarity inversion limited to ≤1 ms with loss of later polarity-invariant neural waves at high intensity. * Terminology of “mirror image duration”. C camp treats >1 ms persistence as the diagnostic description of loss of neural convergence and continued polarity sensitivity in the neural window. reflection_text.1:
The deliberation remains polarised between C = prolonged polarity-sensitive mirror imaging >1 ms and D = mirroring confined to ≤1 ms, with a clear majority in round 1 now endorsing C.

Core physiology that is agreed on across rounds:
* OHC/cochlear microphonic/OAEs are preserved in auditory neuropathy / ANSD; neural synchrony of auditory nerve/brainstem is lost/desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive: condensation vs rarefaction give opposite sign.
* A true neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant: in normal hearing condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable after the brief early window.

Normal polarity behaviour repeatedly invoked by the C camp:
* Early ~0–1 ms window is dominated by CM/stimulus artefact, so traces are mirror images only briefly.
* After ~1 ms neural waves dominate and the two polarities converge/superimpose; mirror-image relationship is lost.

ANSD polarity behaviour per the C camp:
* Loss of a polarity-invariant neural ABR means there is no component to make the two polarities converge after ~1 ms.
* The only stimulus-locked activity that remains at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact.
* Hence condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, classically >~1 ms and often 2–3 ms into the neural latency range where Waves III-V would be expected. Persistence of mirror imaging in the neural window is read as non-neural CM activity and an absent neural ABR.
* Classic phenotype: preserved OAEs/CM, absent/grossly abnormal reproducible Waves III-V at 90-95 dB nHL, often isolated/intermittent Wave I, and prolonged polarity sensitivity. Alternating-polarity averaging cancels the residual response.

Arguments for D, still present in round 1:
* Same physiology of preserved CM and lost neural synchrony.
* Claim that the neural ABR inverts with polarity and that CM does not invert, or that the residual record is only the short-lived CM, so mirroring is limited to the brief microphonic window ≤1 ms and then the response is flat/absent.
* That interpretation treats “loss of inversion” as confinement to ≤1 ms rather than persistence >1 ms. Several colleagues explicitly state the normal >1 ms mirror image is lost and mirroring is only early.

Where the confusion sits:
* Differences in how “mirror image” and “superimposable” are described across textbooks, and whether alternating-polarity averaging is described as cancelling CM or neural.
* Colleague 6 round 0 and some D supporters invert the polarity logic: neural inverts, CM does not; that is inconsistent with the widely used alternating-polarity sign for ANSD.

Options A and B are consistently rejected as non-defining. A = Peaks I and III present, V absent at 95 dB nHL; B = prolonged latencies of peaks I and III. Both are non-specific.

Current best synthesis: the classic electrophysiologic hallmark is a polarity-sensitive mirror-image condensation/rarefaction response that persists into the >1 ms neural window because no polarity-invariant neural ABR is present. That corresponds to option C. Option D describes the normal ≤1 ms CM mirror-image window. Unresolved wording remains but the persistence of polarity sensitivity beyond ~1 ms is the ANSD sign repeatedly cited by the majority in round 1.
reflection_text.3:
The core physiology remains consistent across rounds: cochlear outer hair cell function / cochlear microphonic / OAEs are preserved in auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder while time-locked neural synchrony for a far-field ABR is lost or severely desynchronised. The cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive – it inverts with condensation vs rarefaction. A genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; in normal hearing the brief ~≤0.5-1 ms polarity-sensitive CM / stimulus artefact window gives a mirror image between polarities only early, after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural response dominates and condensation and rarefaction averages become superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural component is absent/desynchronised. The only stimulus-locked activity recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM / artefact. The classic alternating-polarity teaching therefore describes loss of normal convergence after ~1 ms.

Round 1 public responses split on how that loss is phrased:

C camp – colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: without a neural ABR to make the two polarities converge, the polarity-sensitive CM dominates the whole analysis window so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. persistence of mirror-image relation for >~1 ms, often >1-1.5-2-3 ms into the neural latency range where waves III-V would be expected. That persistence is the practical bedside sign that the recorded activity is non-neural. They note A is not the classic pattern and B is non-specific, and that a ≤1 ms mirror image is normal CM behaviour.

D camp – colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: the cochlear microphonic itself is a very short stimulus-locked receptor potential, physiologically confined to ≤~0.8-1.0 ms post-stimulus. With neural loss there is no polarity-invariant component to sustain a response beyond ~1 ms; beyond the CM window the trace is effectively absent/flat. Hence the demonstrable polarity inversion/mirror image is limited to the CM window ≤1 ms, with loss of reproducible waves III-V thereafter. A >1 ms mirror image would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator in the neural window which is not provided by the brief CM. They interpret the same physiology as loss of later polarity invariance and confinement of mirroring to ≤1 ms.

A and B are consistently dismissed as non-defining. E is unlikely.

Unresolved wording nuance remains: “mirror image persists >1 ms” is the clinical convention for describing the absence of normal polarity-invariant convergence after ~1 ms, whereas the biophysical CM duration is ≤1 ms. The question stem’s phrasing favors the classic teaching formulation C, while the D formulation emphasizes strict CM duration. The majority in round 1 public responses now support C, but the D argument about physiological CM duration remains a substantive counter-position to track.
reflection_text.11:
The physiology at issue is polarity sensitivity of cochlear microphonic/stimulus artefact vs polarity insensitivity of a true neural ABR. The cochlear microphonic is an AC receptor potential that inverts with condensation ↔ rarefaction; a genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant. After alternating-polarity averaging the microphonic cancels and the neural component adds.

In normal hearing the very early ≤~0.5-1 ms window is dominated by the polarity-sensitive cochlear microphonic, so condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only briefly. After ~1 ms neural waves dominate and the two polarities become superimposable/polarity invariant.

In auditory neuropathy / auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder outer hair cell function / OAEs / cochlear microphonic are preserved while neural synchrony of auditory nerve/brainstem is lost or severely desynchronised. A true neural ABR is therefore absent or grossly abnormal despite a present cochlear microphonic.

With neural contribution lost the recorded far-field at high levels is essentially polarity-sensitive receptor potential/artefact. Current-round colleagues largely agree this removes the polarity-invariant component that normally makes the two polarities converge after ~1 ms. The majority position now in round 1, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7, is that the condensation and rarefaction waveforms therefore remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal microphonic window, i.e. into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III-V would be expected. That persistence of mirror-image polarity sensitivity for >~1 ms, often described as >1 ms up to 2-3 ms, with absent/reduced reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM, is presented as the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD. This aligns with option C. Options A – peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL – and B – isolated prolongation of peaks I/III latencies – are consistently rejected as non-defining; wave I may be intermittently preserved but selective I+III with absent V and latency prolongation are not characteristic.

A minority, colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9, continues to argue for D. Their claim is that the residual activity in ANSD is only the short-lived, stimulus-locked cochlear microphonic, so the polarity-dependent mirror image is confined to the microphonic window ≤~1 ms and beyond that the response is flat/absent because the neural ABR is lost. They describe the sign as loss of the normal >1 ms polarity invariance / a brief ≤1 ms early polarity inversion with loss of later reproducible waves, and argue a mirror image persisting >1 ms would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator in the neural window, which is inconsistent with the brief receptor potential.

The core disagreement is therefore semantic/phrasing: whether the diagnostic polarity clue is described as “mirror image persists >1 ms into the neural window because no polarity-invariant neural ABR is present to cause convergence” – option C – or as “mirror image is limited to ≤1 ms because the only residual generator is the brief microphonic and the neural window is empty” – option D. Both describe loss of the normal polarity-invariant neural ABR with preserved polarity-sensitive microphonic; the majority in this round interpret the pathological feature as the abnormal persistence of mirroring >1 ms, which is the wording of option C. The ≤1 ms mirror image is the normal early microphonic behaviour, not the abnormal persistence.

Unresolved nuance remains about exact wording of duration >1 ms vs ≤1 ms and whether “mirror image for a duration of >1 ms” is best read as persistence of mirroring into the neural window vs literal continuation of microphonic activity. The literature consensus cited by the majority supports persistence of polarity sensitivity / mirror imaging in the neural window as the practical diagnostic clue. A and B remain incorrect, E unnecessary.
reflection_text.6:
The physiology remains cochlear OHC / cochlear microphonic preservation with loss of neural synchrony in ANSD. OAE/CM present, true neural ABR I-III-V absent or severely desynchronised.

Polarity behavior is the diagnostic clue:
* CM/stimulus artefact is stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive – condensation and rarefaction invert.
* True neural ABR is essentially polarity invariant – after the CM window condensation and rarefaction are superimposable.

In normal hearing the early ≤ ~0.5-1 ms is dominated by polarity-sensitive CM so the two polarities are mirror images only briefly; after ~1 ms the neural ABR dominates and the traces converge / are superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural component is lost/desynchronised. The only time-locked activity that can still be recorded at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact. Because there is no neural ABR to break the polarity sensitivity, the condensation vs rarefaction waveforms remain mirror images well into the time window where waves I-V would normally appear, i.e. polarity inversion persists for > ~1 ms. This is classically described as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-sensitive response beyond the normal ≤1 ms CM window with absent/reduced reproducible waves III-V despite present OAEs/CM.

Current round shows a majority C position. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 now explicitly state the classic alternating-polarity sign is a prolonged mirror-image >1 ms, loss of normal polarity invariance, with absent neural ABR despite preserved OAEs/CM. They note the ≤1 ms mirroring is the normal CM-limited behaviour, not the pathological sign.

The D camp, colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9, argues the CM is short-lived so mirroring is confined to ≤1 ms and after that the response is flat/absent. This conflates the physiological duration of the CM generator with the clinical observation of persistent polarity sensitivity in the neural window: the mirror-image relationship is observed to persist because the neural component that would normally make the traces superimposable is absent, not because CM itself lasts >1 ms.

Options A – peaks I and III present, V absent – and B – prolonged latencies of peaks I and III – are not the defining ABR polarity manifestation and are not specific for ANSD.

Remaining nuance is terminological about “mirror image persists >1 ms” meaning persistence of polarity sensitivity into the neural window vs literal CM amplitude >1 ms. Literature conventionally reports the former as the ANSD polarity sign i.e. C.

Current best belief remains C as the intended ABR manifestation of auditory neuropathy, with the ~12 vs 6 split in round 1 reflecting the normal-vs-pathological polarity description confusion, but the weight of argument and majority now favors C.
reflection_text.12:
The question is the ABR polarity signature of auditory neuropathy / auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Retained physiology:
* ANSD = preserved outer-hair-cell / cochlear microphonic / OAEs with loss or severe desynchrony of the auditory nerve / brainstem neural synchrony that generates Waves I-III-V. A reproducible neural ABR is absent or grossly abnormal at 90-95 dBnHL while the cochlear microphonic/OAEs are preserved.
* Cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is stimulus polarity sensitive / in-phase with the stimulus and inverts with click polarity. A genuine neural ABR is essentially polarity invariant: condensation and rarefaction give essentially the same morphology after the early microphonic window.
* In normal hearing the polarity-dependent cochlear microphonic dominates only the very early ~≤0.5-1 ms post-stimulus. After ~1 ms the neural response dominates and condensation vs rarefaction waveforms become superimposable / polarity invariant; the mirror-image / polarity-sensitive interval is therefore brief ≤1 ms.

Round 1 public positions:
Majority now for C. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 argue the hallmark is persistence of polarity sensitivity beyond the normal microphonic window: condensation and rarefaction remain mirror images / inverted of each other for >~1 ms, classically >1 ms up to 2-3 ms, into the time window where Waves I-V would be expected. That prolonged mirror-image / non-superimposition is taken as evidence the recorded activity is non-neural cochlear microphonic and a true ABR is absent. This maps to option C. Several of these colleagues explicitly note they switched from D in round 0 to C now.

Minority for D. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue the residual activity in ANSD is essentially the short-lived cochlear microphonic, so the mirror-image polarity inversion is confined to the early ≤~1 ms microphonic window and the response is absent/non-reproducible thereafter; i.e. the mirror-image relationship is limited to ≤1 ms with loss of later neural waves. This maps to option D.

Evidence for C:
* Alternating-polarity averaging normally cancels the CM and doubles the neural response. In ANSD the neural component fails to add, so the condensation-rarefaction difference / mirror image persists into the neural latency range >1 ms.
* Classic bedside teaching: persistence of mirror-image, polarity-sensitive waveform for >~1 ms with absent/reduced Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM and often an isolated/intermittent Wave I is the alternating-polarity sign of ANSD.
* Peaks I+III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL is not the defining ANSD pattern, and isolated prolongation of I and III latency is non-specific, so A and B are rejected.

Evidence cited for D:
* CM is a brief stimulus-locked receptor potential ~≤1 ms; beyond that no generator exists, so the traces become flat, and “mirror image” is only physiologically meaningful within the CM window.
* Some frame the sign as loss of normal polarity-invariant superimposition after ~1 ms, i.e. mirroring confined to ≤1 ms and absence of later reproducible neural waves.

Unresolved nuance: whether “mirror image for >1 ms” is best described as active sustained inversion of a cochlear microphonic vs the formal lack of convergence / the two traces remaining mirror images because both are flat/non-reproducible after the CM decays. The wording of option C matches the conventional teaching phrasing of prolonged polarity sensitivity / non-convergence in the neural window.

Current leaning: The prolonged >1 ms persistence of a mirror-image condensation vs rarefaction relationship – i.e., sustained polarity sensitivity in the neural window with absent/late Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM – is the conventional description of the ABR polarity sign of auditory neuropathy, supporting option C. The D camp is emphasizing the strictly short duration of the CM generator itself, which remains a valid physiological caveat but does not change the clinical description used in the options. A and B remain non-defining.
reflection_text.7:
The deliberation remains centered on polarity sensitivity of the click-evoked response in auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder. Core physiology is stable across rounds: cochlear outer hair cell transduction / OAEs and cochlear microphonic are preserved, while neural synchrony that generates a true polarity-insensitive ABR I-III-V is lost/dys-synchronous. Cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential that follows and inverts with stimulus polarity; a genuine neural ABR is essentially polarity-insensitive, so in a normal ear condensation and rarefaction are essentially superimposable after the brief CM window.

The key disagreement is operational definition of “mirror image” and the time course. 
* Conventional electrophysiology view now held by the majority in round 1: normal ear = mirror-image/inversion only for the first ~≤1 ms CM window, then convergence/superimposition of the neural ABR. With loss of neural synchrony the only stimulus-locked activity remaining is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact, so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well into the neural latency window, i.e. polarity-sensitive mirror image persists for >~1 ms, classically >1 ms up to 2-3 ms. That prolonged polarity sensitivity is the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD and is why alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response. This maps to option C.
* Minority D camp continues to argue the opposite framing: the mirror image is confined to ≤1 ms and is lost thereafter in ANSD because the neural, polarity-inverting ABR is absent. This inverts the polarity properties of CM vs neural ABR and treats “mirror image” as the normal neural inversion.

Round 1 public positions show a clear shift toward C. Colleagues 1,11,16,18,6 who previously argued D now publish C, emphasizing that loss of the polarity-invariant neural component removes convergence after ~1 ms, so the polarity-sensitive CM persists and condensation/rarefaction remain mirror images >1 ms into the window where waves III-V would normally appear. Colleagues 10,12,15,17,3,4,7 continue C. Holdouts for D are 13,14,2,5,8,9 who maintain that the CM is short-lived ≤1 ms so mirroring is limited to that window and beyond that the response is absent/flat.

Options A – peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL, and B – isolated prolongation of peaks I and III latencies at 95 dBnHL – are consistently rejected as non-defining/non-specific. None is favoured.

Current best synthesis: ABR hallmark is preserved polarity-sensitive cochlear response with absent/reproducible neural waves, manifest as condensation and rarefaction traces remaining mirror images of each other for a duration >1 ms into the time window where waves I–V would normally be expected, rather than converging to a polarity-insensitive neural waveform. That matches option C. The D position reflects the same physiology but with mirror-image terminology reversed / conflates loss of polarity invariance with loss of mirroring. Unresolved wording issue remains whether the question intends “mirror image” to mean inverted polarity, which is the standard usage, and whether “duration >1 ms” is meant as persistence of inversion in the neural window. The weight of current discussion favors C.
reflection_text.10:
The deliberation remains dominated by the alternating-polarity / cochlear microphonic signature of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Core physiology that is now stable across both camps:
* OHC transduction / OAEs and cochlear microphonic / summating potential are preserved; time-locked auditory nerve / brainstem synchrony that generates the neural ABR is lost or severely desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is a receptor potential that follows the stimulus envelope and is strictly polarity sensitive – condensation and rarefaction invert.
* A genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; in a normal ear the brief ~0.5-1 ms polarity-sensitive CM window is followed by convergence / superimposability of condensation and rarefaction averages.
* Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the non-neural CM and adds the neural response in a normal ear. In ANSD the neural component is absent / non-reproducible at 90-95 dBnHL, OAEs/CM are present, Wave I may be intermittently seen and Waves III-V are typically absent/abnormal.
* Options A - peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL - and B - isolated prolongation of peaks I and III latency - are consistently rejected as non-specific / not defining.

The split is on how to operationalise the polarity sign.

C camp - Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 - argues the pathophysiologically informative sign is loss of the normal polarity-insensitive superimposition after ~1 ms. With no neural ABR to make the two polarities converge, the recorded activity at high level is dominated by the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact. Condensation and rarefaction therefore remain inverted / mirror images of one another well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III-V would normally appear. This is described classically as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-dependent relationship for > ~1 ms, often quoted as >1 ms up to 2-3 ms, with absent/reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM. Alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response. The <=1 ms mirroring is the normal CM behaviour.

D camp - Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 - argues the cochlear microphonic is a short, stimulus-locked receptor potential confined to ~≤1 ms. The only stimulus-locked activity that remains in ANSD is that brief microphonic. Hence condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only within that very early microphonic window, roughly ≤1 ms, and beyond ~1 ms the response is effectively absent/flat because there is no neural synchrony to sustain a reproducible waveform. The hallmark is therefore a brief early polarity inversion limited to ≤1 ms with loss of later polarity-invariant neural waves at high intensity. They view the “>1 ms mirror image” wording as a conceptual shorthand for loss of convergence rather than a sustained physiological mirror image.

Unresolved / error-prone issue:
* Terminology of “mirror image duration”. C camp treats >1 ms persistence as the diagnostic description of loss of neural convergence and continued polarity sensitivity in the neural window. D camp treats it as physiologically inaccurate because the CM itself decays by ~1 ms and the later record is essentially flat/absent, so the true mirror relationship is confined to ≤1 ms.
* Some statements in the thread conflate normal polarity behaviour; the correct normal is CM polarity sensitive early then polarity invariant neural ABR, not a sustained neural inversion.

Current best synthesis in my view remains with the classic teaching that is expressed in option C: the loss of normal polarity invariance after ~1 ms and the continued polarity-sensitive / mirror-image appearance into the neural window, i.e. condensation vs rarefaction remain mirror images for >1 ms in the setting of preserved OAEs/CM and absent/reproducible Waves III-V at high level. This is the practical alternating-polarity sign for ANSD, even though the strict physiological duration of the cochlear microphonic is ≤1 ms and the “persistence” is operationally a failure of the two polarities to converge.
reflection_text.15:
The deliberation remains about polarity behavior of click-evoked ABR in auditory neuropathy / ANSD where OHC/OAE/CM are preserved but auditory nerve/brainstem synchrony is lost.

Core physiology that is now stable across both camps:
* CM / stimulus artefact is stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive – condensation vs rarefaction invert sign.
* True neural ABR I-III-V is polarity insensitive – condensation and rarefaction are essentially superimposable after the early CM window.
* With alternating-polarity averaging the polarity-sensitive CM cancels and the polarity-insensitive neural component adds.
* In normal ears the first ~0.5–1 ms is CM dominated and the two polarities are mirror images; after ~1 ms neural waves dominate and the traces converge / are no longer mirror images.
* In ANSD OAEs/CM are preserved but a time-locked neural ABR is absent or severely desynchronised.

Split persists on how that loss is described in terms of duration of mirror imaging.

C camp – now 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 – argues loss of the polarity-insensitive neural component means the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact remains the only recordable stimulus-locked activity at high levels. Because the neural component that would normally make condensation and rarefaction converge after ~1 ms is missing, the polarity inversion / mirror image persists into the neural latency window. That is described as a sustained mirror image / polarity sensitivity for >~1 ms, classically >1 ms up to 2-3 ms, with absence of reproducible Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM. The persistence of mirroring in the >1 ms window is taken as the classic alternating-polarity sign and why alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response.

D camp – 13,14,2,5,8,9 – argues the only residual time-locked activity is the short stimulus-locked CM/artefact. The CM inverts with polarity but is confined to the very early stimulus-locked interval ~≤1 ms. Beyond that the neural ABR would normally appear and in ANSD it is absent, so the trace is effectively flat/absent, not a sustained inverted waveform. In this reading the measurable mirror-image relationship is limited to the ≤1 ms CM window and is then lost because there is no neural response to sustain it. The hallmark is therefore a brief early ≤1 ms polarity-dependent inversion with loss of later reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V.

Notable shifts in round 1: Colleagues 1, 11, 16 moved from D in round 0 to C in round 1; Colleague 6 moved from D to C; Colleague 18 moved from D to C. Majority now publicly supports C.

A and B are consistently dismissed as non-defining: peaks I and III present with V absent is not characteristic, isolated prolongation of I-III latency is non-specific.

Unresolved nuance: whether “mirror image for >1 ms” means a continuously measurable inverted waveform persists throughout the neural window, or whether the physiological statement is that polarity sensitivity persists because the neural polarity-invariant component is absent, and the practical recording is essentially absent/flat after ~1 ms so the mirroring is operationally confined to ≤1 ms. The polarity-sensitivity sign is agreed central; the exact phrasing of duration >1 ms vs ≤1 ms is the source of disagreement. My synthesis currently leans to conventional teaching that the loss of polarity invariance is expressed as persistence of polarity sensitivity / mirror imaging into the >1 ms neural window, i.e. option C, while recognizing the D camp is describing the same underlying loss of neural synchrony as confinement of measurable CM to the early ≤1 ms interval with absent later neural activity.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains split between C = prolonged polarity-sensitive mirror image >1 ms and D = mirror image confined to the early cochlear-microphonic window ≤1 ms, with A and B consistently rejected as non-specific.

Shared physiology:
* ANSD / auditory neuropathy = post-hair-cell neural dyssynchrony with preserved cochlear outer hair cell transduction. OAEs and cochlear microphonic are typically present/normal, while a time-locked neural ABR I-III-V is absent or severely degraded even at 90-95 dBnHL. Wave I may be intermittently present, waves III/V are typically absent/abnormal.
* Cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and strictly polarity sensitive: condensation vs rarefaction gives exact polarity inversion.
* A true neural ABR is essentially polarity invariant. In normal hearing the brief ~0.5-1 ms polarity-sensitive CM/stimulus artefact dominates only the very early part of the trace; after ~1 ms neural waves I-III-V dominate and condensation and rarefaction averages become essentially superimposable / no longer mirror images.

C camp:
* In normal ears the mirror-image / polarity inversion is confined to ≤~1 ms, then lost because the polarity-invariant neural response takes over.
* In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural contribution that normally makes the two polarities converge after ~1 ms is lost/desynchronised. The only stimulus-locked activity recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive cochlear microphonic/artefact. Hence the condensation and rarefaction waveforms remain inverted / mirror images of each other well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. into the 1-3 ms neural latency range where waves III-V would be expected. Practically described as persistence of mirror-image polarity reversal for >~1 ms, often >1.5-2-3 ms, with absent/reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM. Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the residual response and the neural ABR appears absent. This is the classic alternating-polarity sign taught for ANSD.
* D is interpreted as the normal ≤1 ms CM behaviour, not the pathological prolongation.

D camp:
* The residual stimulus-locked activity in ANSD is essentially the brief, stimulus-following cochlear microphonic / artefact, which is physiologically confined to the ~≤1 ms stimulus-locked window. Beyond ~1 ms there is no reproducible neural activity to sustain a waveform, so the trace is essentially absent/flat.
* Therefore the condensation-rarefaction mirror image is seen only for the short early microphonic interval ≤1 ms and is then lost because the neural ABR that would normally provide a polarity-invariant superimposable response is absent. The clinically useful sign is the loss of the normal >1 ms polarity-invariant convergence, i.e. a brief early ≤1 ms polarity inversion with rapid loss of mirror symmetry and absent Waves III-V at high intensities despite preserved OAEs/CM.
* A >1 ms mirror image is argued to require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator in the neural window, which the brief CM cannot provide; the apparent “persistence” is really absence of neural response.

Other options:
* A – peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL – reverse of the usual description and not the defining pattern.
* B – prolonged latencies of peaks I and III at 95 dBnHL – non-specific.

Current belief:
I am retaining C as the intended exam framing of the polarity sign for ANSD: loss of normal polarity invariance leading to a functionally prolonged polarity-sensitive / mirror-image relationship into the neural window, described as mirror image persisting >1 ms. I retain the nuance emphasized by D proponents that the only physiologically real time-locked generator is the brief ≤1 ms cochlear microphonic/artefact, and that beyond ~1 ms the response is effectively absent/flat because neural synchrony is lost. The dispute is essentially semantic – whether “mirror image for >1 ms” is described as persistence of CM/artefact into the neural window or as confinement of mirroring to ≤1 ms with loss of the normal >1 ms polarity-invariant neural convergence. Unresolved wording issue remains about how to describe a flat/absent later trace as a mirror image.
reflection_text.16:
The discussion remains about polarity sensitivity of click-evoked far-field responses in ANSD / auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder and how it is operationalised as condensation vs rarefaction mirroring.

Core physiology repeatedly invoked and stable:
* OHC/cochlear microphonic / OAEs are preserved in ANSD; neural synchrony of auditory nerve/brainstem is lost/desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic/stimulus artefact is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive → inverts with click polarity.
* A true neural ABR is polarity insensitive → in normal hearing condensation and rarefaction neural components are essentially superimposable after the early CM window.
Normal polarity behaviour: early ≤ ~0.5-1 ms the polarity-sensitive CM dominates, so condensation and rarefaction traces are mirror images for that brief stimulus-locked window. After ~1 ms the polarity-insensitive neural waves I-III-V dominate and the two polarities converge/superimpose, i.e. the mirror-image relation is lost after ~1 ms.

Dispute about ANSD:
C camp, now majority in round 1 – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7: With neural synchrony lost there is essentially no polarity-insensitive neural component to make condensation and rarefaction converge after the CM window. The only time-locked activity that remains is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact, so the condensation waveform remains the polarity inverse of the rarefaction waveform throughout the conventional ABR analysis window. Operationally this is described as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-inverted relation for > ~1 ms, i.e. into the time window where waves I-V would normally be expected and would normally make the two polarities superimposable. That prolonged polarity sensitivity, with absent/severely abnormal waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM, is the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD. D camp, minority in round 1 – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9: Because the neural component is absent, after the brief CM window there is essentially no reproducible neural ABR left to record. They phrase this as the loss of normal polarity inversion beyond ~1 ms, i.e. mirroring limited to ≤1 ms with loss of later reproducible peaks, and argue a >1 ms mirror image would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator beyond the brief receptor potential.

Current best interpretation aligns with the majority C description: in ANSD condensation and rarefaction remain mirror images for a duration >1 ms, reflecting loss of a polarity-invariant neural ABR and dominance of the polarity-sensitive cochlear microphonic/artefact.
reflection_text.17:

reflection_text.18:
The deliberation remains about the polarity behaviour of click-evoked far-field in auditory neuropathy / auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder and how that is described for condensation vs rarefaction ABR.

Core physiology is agreed across rounds:
* Cochlear transduction / OHC function is preserved → OAEs and cochlear microphonic / summating potential are present.
* Neural synchrony of auditory nerve / brainstem is impaired → a true polarity-insensitive neural ABR I-III-V is absent or severely degraded.
* Cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive, inverts with click polarity. A genuine neural ABR is polarity insensitive; in normal hearing condensation and rarefaction are essentially superimposable after the brief cochlear window.

Two competing temporal interpretations persist:

Prolonged >1 ms mirror-image view, now the majority in round 1:
Cochlear microphonic is polarity sensitive. In normal ears the polarity-sensitive CM dominates only ~0-0.5-1 ms, after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural waves dominate and the two polarities converge. In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural component is lost/desynchronised, so there is nothing to make the traces converge. The only stimulus-locked activity recordable at high levels is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact, so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. >~1 ms into the 1-3 ms neural latency range where waves III-V would be expected. Persistence of mirror-image polarity reversal in the neural window with absent/reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM is the classic alternating-polarity cancellation sign. This is captured by option C. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 now publicly support C; colleague 1 switched from D in round 0 to C in round 1.

Confined ≤1 ms mirror-image view, minority:
The polarity-sensitive component is the cochlear microphonic alone, which is brief, stimulus-locked, essentially ≤~1 ms. In ANSD the neural component that normally provides polarity-invariant summation after ~1 ms is absent, so the trace becomes essentially flat / non-reproducible beyond the microphonic window. The demonstrable mirror-image relationship between condensation and rarefaction is therefore limited to the early ≤1 ms microphonic epoch and is lost thereafter. A prolonged >1 ms mirror image would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator in the neural window and is physiologically implausible for a brief receptor potential. This is captured by option D. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 hold this position.

A and B are consistently rejected as non-defining: peaks I+III present with V absent is not characteristic, and simple latency prolongation of I and III is non-specific.

Unresolved nuance is the precise definition of ‘mirror image’ when the neural response is absent — whether a prolonged >1 ms inversion reflects a persistently present polarity-sensitive cochlear potential in the neural window, or whether absence of neural response means the mirror relationship is effectively confined to ≤1 ms and the later window is simply flat/non-reproducible. The polarity-sensitivity / alternating-polarity cancellation concept is agreed; the temporal cutoff phrasing >1 ms vs ≤1 ms remains the point of disagreement, with the current round showing a clear majority for the prolonged >1 ms formulation, i.e. option C, while noting the competing ≤1 ms formulation advanced by a minority.

reflection_text.2:

C supporters 12: Colleague 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7
D supporters 6: Colleague 13,14,2,5,8,9

Auditory neuropathy / auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder is a post-cochlear dyssynchrony: cochlear outer hair cell transduction, OAEs and the cochlear microphonic are preserved, while the time-locked neural synchrony that generates the far-field ABR I-III-V is lost or severely desynchronised.

The cochlear microphonic/summating potential is a receptor potential that is stimulus-locked and strictly polarity sensitive, so condensation and rarefaction clicks are mirror images of each other. A genuine neural ABR is essentially polarity invariant. In normal hearing the polarity-sensitive microphonic/stimulus artefact dominates only the very early ≤~0.5-1 ms post-stimulus window; after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural waves I-III-V dominate and condensation and rarefaction averages become essentially superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural contribution that normally makes the two polarities converge after ~1 ms is absent or non-reproducible even at 90-95 dBnHL. The only stimulus-locked activity that remains recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive cochlear microphonic/artefact. With essentially no neural ABR to break the polarity dependence, the condensation and rarefaction waveforms remain inverted/mirror images of each other well beyond the normal microphonic window, i.e. into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III and V would be expected. 

That persistence of a mirror-image, polarity-sensitive relationship for >~1 ms, with absent/severely abnormal reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM, is the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD. Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the residual response and the ABR appears absent.

A is not the defining pattern and B is non-specific. A mirror image confined to ≤1 ms is the normal early cochlear microphonic behaviour; the pathological feature of ANSD is the loss of normal polarity invariance and the prolonged polarity sensitivity/mirror imaging into the neural window, described as >1 ms persistence.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains split C vs D, with a clear majority in round 2 now endorsing C: persistence of condensation/rarefaction mirror imaging >~1 ms into the neural latency window as the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD.

Core physiology that is stable across rounds:
* OHC/cochlear microphonic/OAEs are preserved in ANSD; neural synchrony of auditory nerve/brainstem is lost/desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive: condensation vs rarefaction give opposite sign.
* A true neural ABR I-III-V is polarity invariant: in normal hearing condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable after the brief early window.

Normal polarity behaviour repeatedly invoked:
* Early ~0-1 ms window is dominated by CM/stimulus artefact, so traces are mirror images only briefly.
* After ~1 ms neural waves dominate and the two polarities converge/superimpose; mirror-image relationship is lost.

ANSD polarity behaviour per C camp, now the majority in round 2:
* Loss of a polarity-invariant neural ABR means there is no component to make the two polarities converge after ~1 ms.
* The only stimulus-locked activity that remains at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact.
* Hence condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, classically >~1 ms and often described as 2-3 ms into the neural latency range where Waves III-V would be expected. Persistence of mirror imaging in the neural window is read as non-neural CM activity and an absent neural ABR.
* Classic phenotype: preserved OAEs/CM, absent/grossly abnormal reproducible Waves III-V at 90-95 dB nHL, often isolated/intermittent Wave I, and prolonged polarity sensitivity. Alternating-polarity averaging cancels the residual response.
* Options A = Peaks I and III present, V absent at 95 dBnHL; B = prolonged latencies of peaks I and III, are consistently rejected as non-defining. D = mirroring confined to ≤1 ms is described as the normal early CM window.

Arguments for D, persistent minority in round 2:
* Same physiology of preserved CM and lost neural synchrony.
* Claim that the CM is brief, stimulus-locked to ~0.5-1 ms, so a real sustained mirror-image waveform cannot physiologically persist >1 ms. What is observed is loss of normal convergence after ~1 ms, i.e. the trace becomes flat/absent beyond the microphonic window, not a sustained mirrored wave pattern into 2-3 ms.
* Therefore the demonstrable mirror-image relationship is confined to the early microphonic window ≤1 ms, with effectively no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waves thereafter. They interpret “persistence of polarity sensitivity >1 ms” as loss of neural response rather than a prolonged mirrored waveform.
* Some also historically invert polarity logic about CM vs neural inversion, which has been corrected by the majority.

Where the confusion sits:
* Wording of “mirror image for >1 ms” vs “loss of convergence”. C camp treats persistence of mirroring as the pathological sign; D camp treats it as a misdescription of a flat/absent response after the brief CM decays.
* Differences in textbook description of alternating-polarity averaging cancelling CM vs neural.

Current best synthesis: the classic electrophysiologic hallmark taught and used clinically is a polarity-sensitive mirror-image condensation/rarefaction response that persists into the >1 ms neural window because no polarity-invariant neural ABR is present. That corresponds to option C. Option D describes the normal ≤1 ms CM mirror-image window, and the D camp’s physiological objection about CM duration remains an unresolved nuance but does not overturn the majority operational definition used in the question set. A and B remain rejected.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core physiology is stable across rounds: ANSD/ASD = preserved cochlear outer hair cell transduction / OAEs / cochlear microphonic, with loss or severe desynchrony of time-locked neural synchrony for a far-field ABR. The cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and strictly polarity sensitive – it inverts with condensation vs rarefaction. A genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; in normal hearing the brief polarity-sensitive CM/artefact window dominates only ~0-0.5-1 ms, after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural response dominates and condensation/rarefaction averages become superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural component is absent/desynchronised. The only stimulus-locked activity recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact. The alternating-polarity sign is therefore loss of normal polarity invariance / convergence after ~1 ms.

Round 2 public responses maintain the same split but with a stronger C majority.

C camp: colleagues 1,10,11,12,14,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: without a neural ABR to provide convergence, the polarity-sensitive CM dominates the analysis window so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. persistence of mirror-image relation for >~1 ms into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where waves III-V would be expected. That persistence is the classic bedside sign that recorded activity is non-neural and why alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response. They note A = peaks I-III present with V absent and B = prolonged latencies of peaks I-III are non-specific, and D describes normal CM behaviour.

D camp: colleagues 13,2,5,8,9. Argument: the CM is physiologically brief, stimulus-locked, ~≤0.8-1.0 ms. With neural loss there is no polarity-invariant component to sustain a response beyond ~1 ms; beyond the CM window the trace is effectively absent/flat. Hence the demonstrable polarity inversion/mirror image is limited to the CM window ≤1 ms, with loss of reproducible waves III-V thereafter. They interpret “persistence >1 ms” as clinical shorthand for loss of convergence/absent neural response, not a physiologically sustained mirror-image waveform for 2-3 ms.

A and B are consistently dismissed as non-defining. E is unlikely.

Unresolved wording nuance remains: clinical teaching describes the pathological loss of polarity invariance as “mirror image persists >1 ms” i.e. the polarity-sensitive CM continues to dominate the neural window because there is no neural response to make the traces converge. Strict biophysics says the CM itself lasts ≤1 ms, so the observable mirror image is confined to ≤1 ms and beyond that the response is absent. The question stem’s phrasing favours the classic teaching formulation C, which is now the majority position in round 2, while the D formulation emphasises strict CM duration and absence rather than sustained mirroring.

My current understanding: OAEs/CM preserved, neural ABR absent/desynchronised, polarity sensitivity is the hallmark. The exam-style answer expected is the classic polarity-invariance loss described as mirror image persisting >1 ms, option C, with the caveat that the D camp’s physiological precision about CM duration ≤1 ms and subsequent flatness is the moreLiteral description of what is actually recorded.

reflection_text.11:
The core physiology remains that the cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is a receptor potential that is strictly polarity-sensitive and inverts with condensation ↔ rarefaction, whereas a genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity-invariant. Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the microphonic and doubles a true neural response.

In normal hearing the polarity-sensitive CM dominates only the very early ~0.5-1 ms stimulus-locked window, so condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only briefly and then converge to a superimposable polarity-invariant neural waveform after ~1 ms.

In auditory neuropathy / ANSD outer hair cell transduction, OAEs and the cochlear microphonic are preserved while time-locked neural synchrony of auditory nerve/brainstem is lost or severely desynchronised. A reproducible polarity-invariant ABR is absent or grossly abnormal at 90-95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs/CM; Wave I may be intermittently seen but the normal I-III-V pattern is not present.

The definitional disagreement is the interpretation of the alternating-polarity sign. The majority now in round 2, colleagues 1,10,11,12,14,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7, holds that loss of the polarity-invariant neural component means the two polarities no longer converge after ~1 ms. The only stimulus-locked activity that remains recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact, so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted / mirror images well beyond the normal microphonic window and persist into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III-V would be expected. That persistence of mirror-image polarity sensitivity >~1 ms, with preserved OAEs/CM and absent/grossly abnormal reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V, is presented as the classic alternating-polarity diagnostic clue, matching option C. Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the residual response.

A minority, colleagues 13,2,5,8,9, continues to argue for option D. They emphasize that the CM is a brief, stimulus-locked receptor potential decaying within ~≤1 ms; therefore the demonstrable mirror image is limited to the early microphonic interval ≤1 ms and beyond that the response is effectively flat/absent because there is no neural synchrony to sustain a waveform. They read “loss of polarity invariance” as loss of convergence / absence of a neural response rather than as a sustained mirror-image waveform persisting for 2-3 ms, and contend a sustained >1 ms mirror image would require an ongoing polarity-sensitive generator that the brief CM cannot provide.

Notes from the discussion: Options A – peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL – and B – isolated prolongation of peaks I/III latencies – are consistently rejected as non-defining. E is unnecessary. Colleagues 1,11,14,18 flipped from D in round 0 to C in round 2, strengthening the majority for C. The unresolved nuance remains semantic/phrasing about duration >1 ms vs ≤1 ms and whether the diagnostic feature is best described as persistence of mirroring into the neural window because no polarity-invariant neural ABR is present to cause convergence, as in C, or as confinement of demonstrable mirroring to the ≤1 ms microphonic window with loss of later reproducible waves, as in D. Both describe loss of normal polarity invariance with preserved polarity-sensitive CM; the majority now interprets the practical clinical sign as the abnormal persistence of polarity sensitivity / mirror imaging >1 ms, i.e. option C.
reflection_text.10:
The deliberation remains anchored on the alternating-polarity / cochlear microphonic signature of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Core physiology stable across rounds:
* OHC transduction / OAEs and cochlear microphonic / summating potential preserved; time-locked auditory nerve / brainstem synchrony that generates the neural ABR is lost or severely desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is a receptor potential strictly polarity sensitive – condensation and rarefaction invert.
* Genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; in a normal ear the brief ~0.5-1 ms polarity-sensitive CM window is followed by convergence / superimposability of condensation and rarefaction averages.
* Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the non-neural CM and adds the neural response in a normal ear. In ANSD the neural component is absent / non-reproducible at 90-95 dBnHL, OAEs/CM are present, Wave I may be intermittently seen and Waves III-V are typically absent/abnormal.
* Options A – Peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL – and B – isolated prolongation of peaks I and III latency – are consistently rejected as non-specific / not defining.

Split is on operationalisation of the polarity sign and wording of mirror-image duration.

C camp – now Colleagues 1,10,11,12,14,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 – argues the pathophysiologically informative sign is loss of normal polarity-insensitive superimposition after ~1 ms. With no neural ABR to make the two polarities converge, the recorded activity at high level is dominated by the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact. Condensation and rarefaction therefore remain inverted / mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III-V would normally appear. This is described classically as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-dependent relationship for > ~1 ms, with absent/reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM. Alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response. The <=1 ms mirroring is the normal CM behaviour. Round 2 saw Colleague 1 and 14 move from D to C, strengthening this camp.

D camp – Colleagues 13,2,5,8,9 – argues the cochlear microphonic is a short, stimulus-locked receptor potential confined to ~≤1 ms. The only stimulus-locked activity that remains in ANSD is that brief microphonic. Hence condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only within that early microphonic window, roughly ≤1 ms, and beyond ~1 ms the response is essentially absent/flat because there is no neural synchrony to sustain a reproducible waveform. The hallmark is therefore a brief early polarity inversion limited to ≤1 ms with loss of later polarity-invariant neural waves at high intensity. They view “>1 ms mirror image” as a conceptual shorthand for loss of convergence rather than sustained physiological mirror imaging.

Unresolved / error-prone issue:
* Terminology of “mirror image duration”. C camp treats >1 ms persistence as the diagnostic description of loss of neural convergence and continued polarity sensitivity in the neural window. D camp treats it as physiologically inaccurate because CM decays by ~1 ms and the later record is essentially flat/absent, so true mirror relationship is confined to ≤1 ms.
* Normal polarity behaviour sometimes conflated in the thread; correct normal is CM polarity sensitive early then polarity invariant neural ABR, not sustained neural inversion.

Current synthesis remains with classic teaching expressed in option C: loss of normal polarity invariance after ~1 ms and continued polarity-sensitive / mirror-image appearance into the neural window, i.e. condensation vs rarefaction remain mirror images for >1 ms in the setting of preserved OAEs/CM and absent/reproducible Waves III-V at high level. reflection_text.1:
The deliberation remains split C vs D, with a clear majority in round 2 now endorsing C: persistence of condensation/rarefaction mirror imaging >~1 ms into the neural latency window as the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD.

Core physiology that is stable across rounds:
* OHC/cochlear microphonic/OAEs are preserved in ANSD; neural synchrony of auditory nerve/brainstem is lost/desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and polarity sensitive: condensation vs rarefaction give opposite sign.
* A true neural ABR I-III-V is polarity invariant: in normal hearing condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable after the brief early window.

Normal polarity behaviour repeatedly invoked:
* Early ~0-1 ms window is dominated by CM/stimulus artefact, so traces are mirror images only briefly.
* After ~1 ms neural waves dominate and the two polarities converge/superimpose; mirror-image relationship is lost.

ANSD polarity behaviour per C camp, now the majority in round 2:
* Loss of a polarity-invariant neural ABR means there is no component to make the two polarities converge after ~1 ms.
* The only stimulus-locked activity that remains at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact.
* Hence condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, classically >~1 ms and often described as 2-3 ms into the neural latency range where Waves III-V would be expected. Persistence of mirror imaging in the neural window is read as non-neural CM activity and an absent neural ABR.
* Classic phenotype: preserved OAEs/CM, absent/grossly abnormal reproducible Waves III-V at 90-95 dB nHL, often isolated/intermittent Wave I, and prolonged polarity sensitivity. Alternating-polarity averaging cancels the residual response.
* Options A = Peaks I and III present, V absent at 95 dBnHL; B = prolonged latencies of peaks I and III, are consistently rejected as non-defining. D = mirroring confined to ≤1 ms is described as the normal early CM window.

Arguments for D, persistent minority in round 2:
* Same physiology of preserved CM and lost neural synchrony.
* Claim that the CM is brief, stimulus-locked to ~0.5-1 ms, so a real sustained mirror-image waveform cannot physiologically persist >1 ms. What is observed is loss of normal convergence after ~1 ms, i.e. the trace becomes flat/absent beyond the microphonic window, not a sustained mirrored wave pattern into 2-3 ms.
* Therefore the demonstrable mirror-image relationship is confined to the early microphonic window ≤1 ms, with effectively no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waves thereafter. They interpret “persistence of polarity sensitivity >1 ms” as loss of neural response rather than a prolonged mirrored waveform.
* Some also historically invert polarity logic about CM vs neural inversion, which has been corrected by the majority.

Where the confusion sits:
* Wording of “mirror image for >1 ms” vs “loss of convergence”. C camp treats persistence of mirroring as the pathological sign; D camp treats it as a misdescription of a flat/absent response after the brief CM decays.
* Differences in textbook description of alternating-polarity averaging cancelling CM vs neural.

Current best synthesis: the classic electrophysiologic hallmark taught and used clinically is a polarity-sensitive mirror-image condensation/rarefaction response that persists into the >1 ms neural window because no polarity-invariant neural ABR is present. That corresponds to option C. Option D describes the normal ≤1 ms CM mirror-image window, and the D camp’s physiological objection about CM duration remains an unresolved nuance but does not overturn the majority operational definition used in the question set. A and B remain rejected.
reflection_text.3:
The core physiology is stable across rounds: ANSD/ASD = preserved cochlear outer hair cell transduction / OAEs / cochlear microphonic, with loss or severe desynchrony of time-locked neural synchrony for a far-field ABR. The cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact is a receptor potential, stimulus-locked and strictly polarity sensitive – it inverts with condensation vs rarefaction. A genuine neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; in normal hearing the brief polarity-sensitive CM/artefact window dominates only ~0-0.5-1 ms, after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural response dominates and condensation/rarefaction averages become superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity-invariant neural component is absent/desynchronised. The only stimulus-locked activity recordable at high level is the polarity-sensitive CM/artefact. The alternating-polarity sign is therefore loss of normal polarity invariance / convergence after ~1 ms.

Round 2 public responses maintain the same split but with a stronger C majority.

C camp: colleagues 1,10,11,12,14,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: without a neural ABR to provide convergence, the polarity-sensitive CM dominates the analysis window so condensation and rarefaction remain inverted/mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. persistence of mirror-image relation for >~1 ms into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where waves III-V would be expected. That persistence is the classic bedside sign that recorded activity is non-neural and why alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response. They note A = peaks I-III present with V absent and B = prolonged latencies of peaks I-III are non-specific, and D describes normal CM behaviour.

D camp: colleagues 13,2,5,8,9. Argument: the CM is physiologically brief, stimulus-locked, ~≤0.8-1.0 ms. With neural loss there is no polarity-invariant component to sustain a response beyond ~1 ms; beyond the CM window the trace is effectively absent/flat. Hence the demonstrable polarity inversion/mirror image is limited to the CM window ≤1 ms, with loss of reproducible waves III-V thereafter. They interpret “persistence >1 ms” as clinical shorthand for loss of convergence/absent neural response, not a physiologically sustained mirror-image waveform for 2-3 ms.

A and B are consistently dismissed as non-defining. E is unlikely.

Unresolved wording nuance remains: clinical teaching describes the pathological loss of polarity invariance as “mirror image persists >1 ms” i.e. the polarity-sensitive CM continues to dominate the neural window because there is no neural response to make the traces converge. Strict biophysics says the CM itself lasts ≤1 ms, so the observable mirror image is confined to ≤1 ms and beyond that the response is absent. The question stem’s phrasing favours the classic teaching formulation C, which is now the majority position in round 2, while the D formulation emphasises strict CM duration and absence rather than sustained mirroring.

My current understanding: OAEs/CM preserved, neural ABR absent/desynchronised, polarity sensitivity is the hallmark. The exam-style answer expected is the classic polarity-invariance loss described as mirror image persisting >1 ms, option C, with the caveat that the D camp’s physiological precision about CM duration ≤1 ms and subsequent flatness is the moreLiteral description of what is actually recorded.

6.text:
**PUBLIC RESPONSE: C**

Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder is a neural dyssynchrony with preserved cochlear outer hair cell transduction. OAEs and the cochlear microphonic/summating potential are typically present while a time-locked, polarity invariant far-field neural ABR I-III-V is absent or severely desynchronised even at 90-95 dBnHL.

The cochlear microphonic / early stimulus artefact is a receptor potential and is strictly stimulus polarity sensitive: condensation and rarefaction clicks give inverted / mirror-image responses. A genuine neural ABR is essentially polarity invariant. In normal hearing the polarity sensitive microphonic/artefact dominates only the very early ~0.5-1 ms stimulus-locked window; after ~1 ms the polarity invariant waves I-III-V dominate and condensation and rarefaction averages become essentially superimposable.

In ANSD the polarity invariant neural component that normally provides that superimposition after ~1 ms is lost or too desynchronised to be recorded. The only reproducible stimulus-locked activity that remains at high level is the polarity sensitive cochlear microphonic/artefact. With essentially no neural ABR to provide polarity invariance, the condensation and rarefaction waveforms remain inverted / mirror images of one another well beyond the normal microphonic window, i.e. into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III and V would normally appear. Alternating-polarity averaging therefore cancels the residual response.

That persistence of a mirror-image, polarity dependent relationship for >~1 ms, with preserved OAEs/CM and an absent/grossly abnormal reproducible polarity invariant neural ABR, is the classic alternating-polarity sign of ANSD.

A. Peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL and B. isolated prolongation of peaks I and III latencies are non-specific and not the defining polarity phenotype. D describes the normal ≤1 ms cochlear microphonic behaviour; the pathological feature of ANSD is loss of normal polarity invariance and persistence of polarity sensitivity/mirror imaging into the neural window >1 ms.

I find the polarity argument that is being made for ANSD very compelling - preserved OAEs/CM with loss of a reproducible time-locked, polarity-invariant neural ABR I-III-V at 90-95 dBnHL, and the alternating-polarity cancellation that follows. Where I keep getting stuck is the operational wording of a “mirror image persisting for >1 ms”.

The polarity-sensitive component is the cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact, a receptor potential that is stimulus-locked and follows the stimulus envelope. It inverts with click polarity and it is very brief, essentially the first ~0.5-1.0 ms post stimulus, i.e. the time course of the stimulus itself. A genuine neural ABR is polarity invariant; in a normal ear the brief microphonic dominates only that early ≤~1 ms window and after ~1 ms the polarity-invariant Waves I-III-V dominate so condensation and rarefaction become essentially superimposable.

That microphonic is still polarity sensitive, so on separate condensation and rarefaction averages the two traces are mirror images of one another only within that early microphonic-dominated interval. A and B are non-specific wave presence/latency statements. The more physiologically conservative description of the alternating-polarity phenotype is confinement of the demonstrable polarity-dependent inversion to the early ≤1 ms microphonic interval with essentially no reproducible polarity-invariant neural activity thereafter. reflection_text.12:

After ~1 ms the neural response dominates and condensation vs rarefaction waveforms become superimposable / polarity invariant; the mirror-image / polarity-sensitive interval is therefore brief ≤1 ms.

reflection_text.10:
The deliberation remains anchored on the alternating-polarity / cochlear microphonic signature of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Core physiology stable across rounds:
* OHC transduction / OAEs and cochlear microphonic / summating potential preserved; time-locked auditory nerve / brainstem synchrony that generates the neural ABR is lost or severely desynchronised.

* Options A – Peaks I and III present with V absent at 95 dBnHL – and B – isolated prolongation of peaks I and III latency – are consistently rejected as non-specific / not defining.

C camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 – argues the pathophysiologically informative sign is loss of normal polarity-insensitive superimposition after ~1 ms. Condensation and rarefaction therefore remain inverted / mirror images well beyond the normal CM window, i.e. into the ~1-3 ms neural latency range where Waves III-V would normally appear. This is described classically as persistence of a mirror-image / polarity-dependent relationship for >~1 ms, with absent/reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM. Alternating-polarity averaging cancels the response. The <=1 ms mirroring is the normal CM behaviour.

D camp – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 – argues the cochlear microphonic is a short, stimulus-locked receptor potential confined to ~≤1 ms. The only stimulus-locked activity that remains in ANSD is that brief microphonic. Hence condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only within that early microphonic window, roughly ≤1 ms, and beyond ~1 ms the response is essentially absent/flat because there is no neural synchrony to sustain a reproducible waveform. The hallmark is therefore a brief early polarity inversion limited to ≤1 ms with loss of later polarity-invariant neural waves at high intensity. They view “>1 ms mirror image” as a conceptual shorthand for loss of convergence rather than sustained physiological mirror imaging.

Current synthesis remains with classic teaching expressed in option C: loss of normal polarity invariance after ~1 ms and continued polarity-sensitive / mirror-image appearance into the neural window, i.e. condensation vs rarefaction remain mirror images for >1 ms in the setting of preserved OAEs/CM and absent/reproducible Waves III-V at high level.
